title: The monkey and the crocodile
hookLine: caught mid-river, the monkey says he left his heart up in the fig tree (Jataka 208)

cards: Sometimes the trouble only shows itself halfway across. The friendly stranger isn't friendly. The deal isn't a deal.
And the only way out is quick thinking. On the bank of the Ganges, the story goes, there lived a monkey, strong and clever. Tradition says it was the Buddha, in an earlier life.
In the river lived a crocodile, whose wife had been watching the monkey leap through the trees. One day she said to her husband: I have a craving. I want to eat that monkey's heart.

teach.h: THE SWEETEST FRUIT ACROSS THE RIVER.
teach.b: The crocodile swims up to the bank, all friendliness. Why stay on this side, eating the same old fruit? Across the river there are mango trees, jackfruit, the sweetest fruit you've ever tasted.
Climb on my back, and I'll take you. That sounds wonderful, and the monkey hops on.
Out in the middle of the river, the crocodile starts to sink. Water up to the monkey's knees. His chest.
Hey, what are you doing? And the crocodile, sure he's won, tells the truth.

teach.h: MY HEART IS IN THE FIG TREE.
teach.b: My wife wants your heart. I'm going to drown you and bring it to her. The monkey can't fight.
He can't swim to shore. So he laughs. Oh, friend, you should have said so!
We monkeys don't keep our hearts inside us when we're out and about. We'd smash them to pieces, jumping from branch to branch.

teach.h: A CALM MIND IN DEEP WATER.
teach.b: We hang them up in a tree for safekeeping. See that fig tree, with all the round fruit hanging on it? Those are our hearts.
Take me back and I'll give you mine. The crocodile, not the brightest, swims back to the bank. The monkey leaps off, up into the fig tree, and calls down: you big fool.
Did you really think anyone keeps his heart in a treetop?
You're huge, but you have no wits at all. What makes this one lovely is where the monkey's strength came from. Not muscles.
Not claws. A calm mind, in deep water, that saw a way out force could never find.

how: The monkey and the crocodile is told to children in Buddhist homes and schools, appears in early Buddhist carving, and is found in the Panchatantra as well.

o: a crocodile, the big river beast
the fig tree on the far bank
a clever monkey on the riverbank

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the promise of the sweetest fruit
where the monkey said his heart hung

s: the monkey escaped by fighting the crocodile
he stayed calm and talked his way out: my heart is in the fig tree.
the crocodile wanted the monkey's heart for his wife
she had a craving for it.
this story is told in more than one collection
it's in the Jataka, and a version is in the Panchatantra.

games.q: you're a monkey in the middle of a river, on a crocodile's back. he's sinking, and says he wants your heart. what do you do?
o: jump off and try to swim.
tell him your heart is back in the fig tree.
beg him to let you go.
games.why: the monkey laughs and says monkeys keep their hearts in trees. the crocodile swims back, and the monkey leaps to safety.

practice: Pick a situation where you usually push: an argument, a negotiation, a kid who won't put their shoes on.
Picture yourself in the middle of the river with it, and instead of struggling, take one slow breath and ask: what's another way out? A joke, a question, a different door; let an idea come.

wordCard.voice: Sumsumara. The crocodile who tricked the monkey into deep water, until the monkey stayed calm, said his heart was in the fig tree, and got away.

orig.note: Pali: crocodile. The story is the Sumsumara Jataka.

carryVoice: Your line: keep your wits. The crocodile was huge; the monkey was quick. That's day eighty-nine.
